title: The Eastern Governorship
notebook: Pavel Kasic: Halvek's appointee as governor of Sevagrad. Competent on the border. Answers to the Interior Ministry.
Mira Brana: retired garrison colonel. Knows every pass on the eastern border. Iron Covenant sympathies.
Ivo Lenart: Sevagrad lawyer. Ten years in the border courts defending refugee families. Little administrative experience.

narrative.text: The garrison town of Sevagrad sits where the valley narrows, and the wind comes down off the mountains carrying grit from the Morivask plains. Soldiers in grey greatcoats stand at the gate and do not speak. Above the roofs the Korengal pass cuts a pale notch through the ridge, and you can see the road climbing toward it in switchbacks, a thin line of trucks moving slowly up the grade. The Governor's Residence is a stone house behind a wall, built in the years when Halvek wanted the frontier to look like a fortress from the road.

I have governed this province through every crisis Halvek's office chose not to name, Chancellor. I have never once been asked what the border needs. The supply line to the garrisons was rerouted twice by people who have never driven a truck on it. The reception posts at the crossing were designed for a different century of traffic. I wrote to the Interior Ministry about each of these things, and the replies were polite and empty.

I am not asking you to keep me out of loyalty to Halvek. I am asking because the crossing works, mostly, and the people who run it know their jobs. If you replace me, you will be swapping a man who knows where the water pipes run under the Korengal road for someone who has to learn that from a clerk. Do what you think is right. But do it knowing what the border costs when the person in charge changes in a month.

Kasic stands, buttons his coat, and offers his hand. His grip is dry and brief. At the door he pauses to look at the wall map on the far side of the room, the eastern provinces in faded ink, the pass marked with a small cross that someone added by hand years ago. Then he is gone, and the room is quiet except for the wind against the shutters and the sound of Vyktor turning a page in his folder.

He was competent, and he was Halvek's, and both of those are true, so do not let me simplify him for you. The border is the worst place in Veltria to find out whether a new appointee can learn fast enough. But here is the rest of the file. Kasic answers, in the end, to an Interior Ministry that still takes calls from the networks that placed him. If you keep him, you keep a channel you cannot see into. If you replace him, the question is not whether the replacement is good. The question is who chose him and by what route.

The press will read a replacement by decree in one way only. Halvek appointed every governor in this country for twenty-three years. A new Chancellor removing a provincial governor with her own signature will be described, in every paper that matters, as the same thing with a different face. I am not telling you not to do it. I am telling you what the headlines will say before the ink is dry.

Mira Brana comes in from the courtyard with mud on her boots and does not sit until she has looked at the map. She is in her sixties, retired from the garrison, with a soldier's economy of movement and a face that has spent a long time squinting into weather. She knows every pass on this border. You can see it in the way her finger finds the Korengal road without searching for it.

I have walked every pass between this town and the Morivask line, Chancellor, most of them twice. I can tell you which ones a truck can take in February and which ones a child can take in a blizzard. The Covenant men will tell you I am their candidate. They may be right about the first part and wrong about the reason. I want the crossing run by someone who will not let the garrison and the camps fight over the same road.

I have no illusions about who is on that road. Some of the people crossing are fleeing, and some of them are not. The men who watch the passes decide who gets through, and I would rather those decisions were made by people who know the ground than by a ministry that has never seen it. I will not pretend that is a comfortable answer. It is the one I can carry out.

Ivo Lenart arrives last, out of breath from the stairs, with a folder under one arm that has come apart at the corner. He is a decade younger than the others and still wears the ink-stained cuffs of a lawyer who has spent late nights in border courts. He apologizes for being late and does not apologize again for anything else. Through the window behind him, the Korengal road climbs toward the pass in the afternoon light.

For ten years I stood in the border courts and watched families lose their cases because the paperwork was in the wrong language, or a clerk was tired, or nobody had told them they could appeal. I know what this province does to people who have nothing but a file and a claim. I am not an administrator. I have never run anything larger than my own office. But I know what the law says, and the law says these people have a right to be heard before they are turned back at the river.

The camps need someone who will open doors, and I will open them. The school buildings in the two market towns are empty until spring. I could have families in them by the end of the week if someone signs the requisition. I know what the Interior Ministry will say about that. I would rather hear it from you than read it in a newspaper.

Three people, and each of them holds a true version of the border. Kasic knows the pipes and the supply lines. Brana knows the passes. Lenart knows the cases that never reached the Ministry. The job will look the same from the Chancellor's chair whichever of them you choose. The question is which failure you are prepared to be asked about in public, and which family you will have to explain to, if you are wrong.

monologue: Three people want the eastern border. Kasic is competent and answers to Halvek's networks. Brana knows every pass and carries Covenant sympathies. Lenart has spent a decade defending the families who wait at the river, and has never run anything large.

choices.text: "Keep him. For now. He has run this border through every crisis Halvek's office refused to name, and I will not replace the one man who knows where the water runs. I want weekly reports, and I want to know who he calls."

reactions.text: Vyktor closes his folder. He does not smile. He says the Interior Ministry will be pleased, and he says it in the tone of a man who has noted that the pleasure belongs to someone else.
Lenart says nothing. He writes the decision on the back of his folder and underlines the words for now.

choices.text: "Appoint Mira Brana as governor. She knows the passes, she knows the garrisons, and she will hold the crossing. I am not appointing her to please the Covenant. I am appointing her because she is the one who can do the job."

reactions.text: Brana nods once, the way a soldier acknowledges an order she expected. She is already asking about the garrison rolls, the vehicle pool, and which companies she can move to the crossing without leaving the passes open.
Vyktor is quiet for a moment. Then he says the press will call it a new appointment by decree, and he says it without argument, because he has already drafted the answer.

choices.text: "Appoint Ivo Lenart as governor. Open the border courts and the camps to the families who have been waiting at the river. Let the province see what a governor who listens looks like."

reactions.text: Lenart stands too fast and knocks the folder off the table. He gathers the pages and does not apologize for it. He is already asking who in the Interior Ministry he can call before the end of the day.
Vyktor says the decision will be read in Sevagrad as a judgment on Halvek's governors, and in Republic Square as the first act of a new one. He says it as a fact, not as an objection.
